title: Wi-Fi 6, 6E and 7 explained: what each generation adds
metaDescription: How Wi-Fi 6, Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 differ, what the 6GHz band and multi-link operation do, and whether upgrading your router will make a difference.
excerpt: Router boxes now advertise Wi-Fi 7. Here is what each generation adds, what your devices need to benefit, and when an upgrade is worth it.
_note: AI-assisted draft from public sources. Check every fact, add your own experience and photos, then publish from /studio.
answer: Wi-Fi 6 handles many devices at once more efficiently. Wi-Fi 6E adds the 6GHz band, which is less crowded and offers wider channels. Wi-Fi 7 adds 320MHz channels, faster 4096-QAM modulation and multi-link operation, which uses several bands at once. You only benefit if your phones and laptops support the same generation.

sections.heading: Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax)
sections.body:
Wi-Fi 6 was designed for busy networks. Its headline feature, OFDMA, lets a router split a channel into smaller pieces and serve several devices in a single transmission instead of making them take turns. Combined with improvements to MU-MIMO and a power-saving feature called target wake time, it keeps networks responsive when dozens of phones, laptops, speakers and smart plugs are connected.

Wi-Fi 6 works on the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands, like earlier generations. Most phones and laptops from recent years support it.

sections.heading: Wi-Fi 6E: the 6GHz band
sections.body:
Wi-Fi 6E is Wi-Fi 6 extended into the 6GHz band. In the UK, Ofcom has opened part of this band for Wi-Fi. The 6GHz band is much less crowded than 5GHz, since only newer devices can use it, and supports wide 160MHz channels for high speeds.

The trade-off is range. Higher frequencies are absorbed more by walls and floors, so 6GHz works best in the same room as the router or with mesh points close by.

sections.heading: Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be)
sections.body:
Wi-Fi 7 builds on 6E with several changes:

- **320MHz channels** in the 6GHz band, double the maximum width, where spectrum allows. In the UK the amount of 6GHz spectrum available limits how often full 320MHz channels can be used.
- **4096-QAM** modulation, packing 12 bits into each symbol instead of 10, about 20 per cent more throughput in strong signal conditions.
- **Multi-link operation (MLO),** which lets a device connect over two or more bands at once, for higher speed, lower latency and a more reliable connection when one band suffers interference.

The theoretical maximum speeds are enormous, but real-world gains depend on distance, walls and your devices.

sections.heading: Will upgrading help?
sections.body:
A new router only helps if something on your network is the bottleneck:

- **Broadband speed:** if your connection is 70Mbps, any Wi-Fi 5 or Wi-Fi 6 router can already deliver it to a nearby device. Faster Wi-Fi helps with full fibre of 500Mbps and above.
- **Coverage:** if Wi-Fi is slow in far rooms, a mesh system or better placement helps more than a newer standard.
- **Your devices:** a laptop with Wi-Fi 6 connects at Wi-Fi 6 speeds to a Wi-Fi 7 router. You gain the newest features only as you replace devices.
- **Busy homes:** many connected devices benefit from Wi-Fi 6 or later.

Routers are backwards compatible, so older devices keep working on a new router.

sections.heading: Buying advice
sections.body:
- If your router is Wi-Fi 5 or older and your home has many devices or fast broadband, Wi-Fi 6 or 6E is a solid upgrade.
- Choose Wi-Fi 7 if you have recent devices that support it, fast broadband, and want the router to last several years.
- Look at mesh options for larger homes.
- Check the security update period, as routers sit at the edge of your network and need ongoing updates.

faq.a: Only if you have fast broadband and recent devices that support it. Otherwise a good Wi-Fi 6 or 6E router, well placed, will perform similarly.

faq.q: Will a Wi-Fi 7 router work with older devices?
faq.a: Yes. Wi-Fi routers are backwards compatible, so older phones and laptops connect using the standards they support.
